query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the substrate during the additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce thermal gradients during solidification, leading to a more homogeneous microstructure with fewer defects, lower residual stresses, and improved mechanical integrity compared to processing on a room‐temperature substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high‐entropy alloy powder feedstock that, when conventionally processed, is prone to compositional segregation, high residual stress, and defect formation.
generation.intervention: Introduce an elevated substrate/powder-bed temperature (e.g., in the range of 200–500°C) during laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.
generation.conditions: Identical laser processing parameters (e.g., scanning speed, laser power, atmosphere) used in additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi, with the only variable being the substrate/powder bed temperature, under typical lab-scale build sizes.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic diffusion during solidification due to moderated cooling rates, leading to a more uniform distribution of elements and alleviation of thermal stress gradients.
generation.mechanism: Preheating reduces the steep thermal gradients between the melt pool and the substrate, which decreases rapid cooling and contraction. This controlled cooling permits a more uniform diffusion of alloying elements during solidification, minimizing segregation and reducing the development of residual stresses and related defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: The preheated builds will exhibit lower levels of microsegregation, reduced residual stress (as measured by XRD or neutron diffraction), fewer processing defects (verified via CT scanning or microscopy), and improved mechanical performance (e.g., higher yield strength and ductility) relative to samples processed at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Conventional additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi using room-temperature substrate conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be observable under controlled laser powder bed fusion conditions with the specified preheat temperature range. The hypothesis is primarily applicable at lab-scale builds; scale-up and variations in laser parameters may necessitate additional tuning.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheat temperature for achieving the best balance between reducing thermal gradients and avoiding unintended microstructural changes is not precisely known. Effects on long-term performance and industrial-scale builds also remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples via laser powder bed fusion: one set with a preheated substrate (e.g., maintained at 300°C as a representative condition within the proposed range) and one set with a room-temperature substrate. Characterize both sets using microstructural imaging (e.g., SEM, EDS mapping for segregation), residual stress measurements (using XRD or neutron diffraction), defect quantification (via CT scanning), and mechanical testing (tensile tests and impact toughness).
measurements: Grain uniformity and microsegregation levels (SEM, EDS analysis)
Residual stress profiles (XRD or neutron diffraction)
Mechanical properties including yield strength and ductility (tensile tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If preheated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in microstructural homogeneity, a reduction in residual stress and defect density, or enhanced mechanical properties compared to the room-temperature samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
